Folding and trimming

Source: vignettes/folding.Rmd
folding.Rmd
library(multimod)
mod <- example_models$energyRt$multimod
mod
#> Model: 
#> Source:  C:/Users/admin/Documents/R/energyRt/gams/energyRt.gms 
#> Language:  GAMS 
#> Sets:  27 
#> Mappings:  324 
#> Aliases:  7 
#> Parameters:  218 
#> Variables:  93 
#> Equations:  153

The flexibility-performance tradeoff

Framework models such as energyRt are written for maximum flexibility: one generic set of equations covers technologies, storage, trade, emissions and more, and every parameter is indexed over every dimension it could ever vary by (technology, commodity, region, year, timeslice). A given scenario uses only part of that:

  • a single-region model has no interregional trade,
  • most technologies have the same efficiency in every timeslice,
  • features the scenario does not use leave sets and mappings empty, and the equations that depend on them generate no constraints.

The flexibility is paid for at model-build time and in the solver: data that is repeated across a dimension inflates the data files and the coefficient count, and equations with empty domains are still processed. multimod offers two complementary transformations that remove this redundancy without changing the optimum:

  1. Folding removes a dimension from a parameter when the values are constant across it (data redundancy).
  2. Trimming marks sets, parameters, mappings, variables and equations that have no data or no instances, so code generators skip them (structural redundancy).

Both are reversible and both are honoured by every writer and by the direct matrix route.

Folding

The idea

Take a 5-dimensional parameter whose values do not depend on the timeslice:

pTechCinp2use[E01, ELC, R1, 2025, s1] = 0.95
pTechCinp2use[E01, ELC, R1, 2025, s2] = 0.95
...

Folding drops the timeslice dimension and keeps one row per remaining index combination. Equations that reference the parameter are rewritten to omit the folded index:

# before
vTechInp[t,c,r,y,s] >= pTechCinp2use[t,c,r,y,s] * vTechAct[t,r,y,s]
# after
vTechInp[t,c,r,y,s] >= pTechCinp2use[t,c,r,y]   * vTechAct[t,r,y,s]

Diagnose redundancy

analyze_parameter_redundancy() reports, per parameter, how many rows carry a repeated value. High redundancy marks a folding candidate.

red <- analyze_parameter_redundancy(mod, verbose = FALSE)
red <- red[order(-red$orig_redundancy_pct), ]
head(red[, c("param_name", "dims", "orig_rows", "orig_unique",
             "orig_redundancy_pct")], 8)
#>          param_name                                   dims orig_rows
#> 3     pTechCinp2use    tech, comm, region, year, timeslice      1344
#> 30      pTradeIrEff trade, region, region, year, timeslice       576
#> 8         pTechAfLo          tech, region, year, timeslice       336
#> 23   pStorageInpEff     stg, comm, region, year, timeslice       336
#> 24   pStorageOutEff     stg, comm, region, year, timeslice       336
#> 20    pTimesliceAgg             year, timeslice, timeslice       180
#> 19 pTimesliceWeight                        year, timeslice        68
#> 35    pTradeInvcost                    trade, region, year        48
#>    orig_unique orig_redundancy_pct
#> 3            3                99.8
#> 30           1                99.8
#> 8            1                99.7
#> 23           1                99.7
#> 24           1                99.7
#> 20           1                99.4
#> 19           1                98.5
#> 35           1                97.9

Build a fold specification

create_fold_spec() takes fold_dims, a named list: one entry per dimension to fold, whose value names the validation mappings to check against. For an energyRt model the technology parameters are validated against mTechTimeslice and the commodity parameters against mCommTimeslice:

fold_spec <- create_fold_spec(
  mod,
  fold_dims = list(
    timeslice = list(tech = "mTechTimeslice", comm = "mCommTimeslice")
  ),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fold_spec[, c("param_name", "validation_mapping", "can_fold", "unproven")]
#>         param_name validation_mapping can_fold unproven
#> 1    pTechCinp2use     mTechTimeslice     TRUE    FALSE
#> 2        pTechAfLo     mTechTimeslice     TRUE    FALSE
#> 3         pSupCost     mCommTimeslice     TRUE    FALSE
#> 4 pTimesliceWeight               <NA>     TRUE    FALSE
#> 5    pTimesliceAgg               <NA>    FALSE    FALSE
#> 6   pStorageInpEff     mCommTimeslice     TRUE    FALSE
#> 7   pStorageOutEff     mCommTimeslice     TRUE    FALSE
#> 8      pTradeIrEff               <NA>    FALSE    FALSE
#> 9  pImportRowPrice               <NA>    FALSE     TRUE

The result is a data frame with one row per parameter that carries the dimension. can_fold is TRUE when the values are constant across the dimension in every group formed by the other indices. unproven flags parameters that failed only because no validation mapping was found for their entity type; supplying one (for example sup = "mSupTimeslice") would let them be checked.

Why validate against a mapping? A parameter may be constant across the timeslice in the data only because the scenario never varied it. The mapping says which entities are allowed to vary by that dimension, so folding stays consistent with the model structure, not just with one dataset. A value of c("mStorageComm", "mCommTimeslice") chains two mappings when the entity is linked to the dimension indirectly.

Several dimensions can be folded in one specification; they are applied in the order given, each on the result of the previous one:

create_fold_spec(
  mod,
  fold_dims = list(
    timeslice = list(tech = "mTechTimeslice", comm = "mCommTimeslice"),
    region    = list(comm = "mCommRegion")
  )
)

Apply the fold 

mod_folded <- fold_model(mod, fold_spec = fold_spec, verbose = FALSE)
is_folded(mod)
#> [1] FALSE
is_folded(mod_folded)
#> [1] TRUE

fold_model() collapses the data of every parameter with can_fold = TRUE, rewrites each equation that references one of them, and records what it did in model$misc$fold_summary. get_fold_summary() reads that record:

get_fold_summary(mod_folded, format = "data.frame")[
  , c("parameter", "removed_dims", "original_rows", "folded_rows", "compression")]
#>          parameter removed_dims original_rows folded_rows compression
#> 1    pTechCinp2use    timeslice          1344         112       12.0x
#> 2        pTechAfLo    timeslice           336          28       12.0x
#> 3         pSupCost    timeslice            76          76        1.0x
#> 4 pTimesliceWeight    timeslice            68           4       17.0x
#> 5   pStorageInpEff    timeslice           336          28       12.0x
#> 6   pStorageOutEff    timeslice           336          28       12.0x

With format = "text" the same information is printed as a report; format = "list" returns it as nested lists.

Inspect a folded parameter

is_folded() also works on a single parameter, and get_active_dims() returns the dimensions in force after folding; the declaration stays in $dims.

p <- mod_folded$parameters$pTechCinp2use
is_folded(p)
#> [1] TRUE
p$dims              # as declared
#> <AST dims> 
#> [tech,comm,region,year,timeslice]
get_active_dims(p)  # in force after folding
#> <AST dims> 
#> [tech,comm,region,year]

# parameters the fold did not touch keep their declaration
is_folded(mod_folded$parameters$pTechInvcost)
#> [1] FALSE

The fold metadata lives in p$misc$fold_info:

p$misc$fold_info[c("original_dims", "removed_dims", "original_rows",
                   "folded_rows", "compression_ratio")]
#> $original_dims
#> [1] "tech"      "comm"      "region"    "year"      "timeslice"
#> 
#> $removed_dims
#> [1] "timeslice"
#> 
#> $original_rows
#> [1] 1344
#> 
#> $folded_rows
#> [1] 112
#> 
#> $compression_ratio
#> [1] 12

Unfold

unfold_model() restores the original data and dimensions of every folded parameter:

mod_unfolded <- unfold_model(mod_folded, verbose = FALSE)
nrow(mod_unfolded$parameters$pTechCinp2use$data)
#> [1] 1344
nrow(mod$parameters$pTechCinp2use$data)
#> [1] 1344

Aliases and repeated dimensions

A parameter can be declared with one dimension name while its data uses an alias column (comm declared, acomm in the data), or a dimension can appear twice in different roles ({region, region} stored as src, dst). Folding resolves the first through model$aliases and keeps every data column other than the folded one for the second, so both cases fold without special handling.

Trimming

The idea

A scenario rarely exercises every feature of a framework model. Elements that end up without data or without instances are:

  • empty sets and mappings (no storage technologies, no trade routes),
  • empty parameters,
  • variables indexed by an empty set,
  • equations whose domain is empty, or that only reference trimmed variables.

Trimming marks these with $trimmed = TRUE. Nothing is deleted; code generators and write_latex() check the flag and skip (or annotate) the element.

Four phases 

1. mark sets, parameters and mappings with no data
2. mark variables whose domain is empty
3. mark equations with an empty domain, or with only trimmed variables
4. untrim anything a non-trimmed equation still uses

Phase 4 is what keeps trimming conservative: an element is only trimmed when no surviving equation needs it.

Apply the trim

Fold first, then trim: folding can empty a parameter that trimming then removes.

mod_trimmed <- trim_model(mod_folded, verbose = FALSE)
is_trimmed(mod)
#> [1] FALSE
is_trimmed(mod_trimmed)
#> [1] TRUE
get_trim_summary(mod_trimmed, format = "data.frame")
#>   element_type total trimmed remaining percent_trimmed
#> 1         sets    27       6        21            22.2
#> 2   parameters   218       1       217             0.5
#> 3     mappings   324     160       164            49.4
#> 4    variables    93      10        83            10.8
#> 5    equations   153     103        50            67.3

The example scenario uses a small share of the energyRt equations, so most of them trim away. As with folding, format = "text" prints a report and format = "list" returns nested lists. is_trimmed() works on individual elements too:

is_trimmed(mod_trimmed$equations$eqTechCap)
#> [1] FALSE
is_trimmed(mod_trimmed$equations$eqTechInpTot)
#> [1] FALSE
head(get_trim_summary(mod_trimmed, format = "list")$equations$names)
#> [1] "eqTechGrp2Sng"    "eqTechSng2Grp"    "eqTechGrp2Grp"    "eqTechShareInpLo"
#> [5] "eqTechShareInpUp" "eqTechShareOutLo"

Untrim

untrim_model() clears the flags, on all element types by default or on the ones named in elements:

mod_back <- untrim_model(mod_trimmed)
is_trimmed(mod_back)
#> [1] FALSE

Folding versus trimming

Folding Trimming
Targets data redundancy structural redundancy
Mechanism collapses a constant dimension flags unused elements
Reduces parameter rows, coefficient count sets, parameters, variables, equations emitted
Needs a fold specification (validation mappings) nothing; driven by the data
Reversed by unfold_model() untrim_model()

Fold when parameters are constant across a dimension the scenario does not need (timeslice is the usual case), when data files or solver memory are the bottleneck, or when a model written for many regions or years is run with one.

Trim when the scenario leaves optional features unused, when empty sets or parameters exist, or when many equations generate no constraints.

Do both for framework models: fold first, then trim. Check that the objective is unchanged before relying on a transformed model (see the appendix).

Folding and trimming change what the generated model contains; they do not change what it means. Do not fold a dimension that genuinely varies in the data (create_fold_spec() refuses, but a hand-edited specification can override it), and keep an untrimmed copy when the complete structure is wanted for documentation or comparison.

Writing transformed models

Every writer honours the flags. write_gmpl(), write_jump() and write_pyomo() use the folded dimensions by default and skip trimmed elements; write_latex() chooses model_view = "reduced" for a folded or trimmed model and annotates the removed elements in model_view = "full". model_to_lp() and solve_highs() assemble the matrix from the active dimensions directly.

dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "trimmed")
save_model(mod_trimmed, dir, format = "ipc")
write_gmpl(mod_trimmed, model_dir = dir)
write_jump(mod_trimmed, model_dir = dir)
write_latex(mod_trimmed, file = file.path(dir, "model.tex"), model_view = "full")

A fold specification is an ordinary data frame; save it with saveRDS() to reproduce the transformation on another scenario of the same model.

Limitations

  • Folding is all-or-nothing per parameter: either every group is constant across the dimension or the parameter is left alone.
  • Folding needs validation mappings that reflect the model’s structure; for a non-energyRt model, name the mappings that link each entity to the dimension.
  • Folding loads the parameter data into memory while it runs.
  • Trimming only flags elements; the data stays on disk and in the object.
  • Trimming is conservative by design: it never removes an element a surviving equation references, so unused variables inside non-empty equations are kept.

Appendix: the objective is unchanged

The transformed models must solve to the same objective as the original. The check below uses the in-process HiGHS route; it is not run when the vignette is built because it needs the highs package and takes a few seconds.

r0 <- solve_highs(mod, attach = FALSE)
r1 <- solve_highs(mod_folded, attach = FALSE)
r2 <- solve_highs(mod_trimmed, attach = FALSE)
c(original = r0$objective, folded = r1$objective, trimmed = r2$objective)
all.equal(r0$objective, r1$objective)
all.equal(r0$objective, r2$objective)
